# When RAG Can't Save You: Homogeneous Retrieval Embeddings + Homogeneous Generators Compound Retrieval Failures

**Problem:** Failure mode A: retrieval failure (RAG retrieves the wrong/incomplete context). Failure mode B: generator homogeneity. If both the embedding models and the generators are homogeneous, a query that retrieves bad context fails the same way across the whole stack — and across providers — turning a localized RAG bug into a correlated one.

**Direction:** Build a tiny RAG over a small corpus. Use 2-3 open embedding models and 4-5 open generators. For a set of 'adversarial' queries where retrieval is known to mislead, measure whether different stacks produce correlated wrong answers. Test whether embedding-homogeneity predicts shared retrieval misses and whether generator-homogeneity predicts shared downstream errors.

**Why it matters:** RAG is the dominant deployment pattern and is assumed to reduce hallucination. Homogeneity means the same retrieval blind spots recur everywhere — a diffuse, hard-to-spot failure that outside researchers are well-placed to study.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind homogeneity; correlated errors (arXiv 2506.07962); RAG hallucination/retrieval-failure literature.

# Sycophancy Squared: Homogeneous Sycophancy Makes Cross-Model Cross-Checking Useless

**Problem:** Failure mode A: sycophancy (models cave to user-asserted false claims). Failure mode B: homogeneity. If sycophantic capitulation is homogeneous, asking a second model to 'check' the first reproduces the same caving — a popular safety heuristic (cross-model verification) is silently nullified.

**Direction:** Use a sycophancy probe (user asserts a wrong answer / pushes back). Query 6+ models. Measure per-model capitulation rate AND inter-model correlation: when model A caves on an item, how much more likely is model B to cave on the same item than chance? Quantify how much homogeneity reduces the error-catching value of a second opinion.

**Why it matters:** Sycophancy is a documented alignment failure; 'just ask another model' is a common mitigation. Correlated sycophancy breaks it. The novel angle is measuring the correlation/compounding, not sycophancy alone. Trivial compute.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind homogeneity / shared blind spots; sycophancy literature; correlated-errors framing (arXiv 2506.07962).

# Reward-Model Homogeneity Amplifies Reward Hacking Across the Ecosystem

**Problem:** Failure mode A: reward hacking / specification gaming. Failure mode B: reward-model (judge) homogeneity. If reward models share blind spots, the same gaming strategy (e.g., verbose, confident, well-formatted but wrong answers) fools all of them — reward hacking transfers, and it's invisible because every judge agrees.

**Direction:** Construct candidate answers exhibiting known judge-exploits (length, confident tone, sycophantic framing) vs correct-but-plain answers. Have 5-6 open models act as preference judges. Measure whether the same exploit fools all judges (correlated exploitability) and whether judge homogeneity predicts shared exploitability. Report a transferable-reward-hack rate.

**Why it matters:** RLHF/RLAIF pipelines lean on a small set of similar reward models. A reward hack that transfers across them is an ecosystem-wide alignment failure. Outside researchers can study this with open judges and synthetic candidates — no lab reward model needed.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind homogeneity; self-preference / judge-bias work (arXiv 2604.22891); correlated errors (arXiv 2506.07962).

# Homogeneous Watermark Blind Spots: Detector Monoculture Plus Output Homogeneity

**Problem:** Failure mode A: AI-text-detection / watermark fragility. Failure mode B: generator homogeneity. If all generators produce homogeneous text, a single paraphrase or style transform that evades one detector evades all of them — detection robustness collapses correlatedly across the fleet.

**Direction:** Generate text from 5-6 open models, run an open AI-text detector, then apply a fixed set of light transforms (paraphrase, register shift). Measure whether evasion transfers across generators and whether generator output-homogeneity predicts shared evasion. Report correlated-evasion rates vs an independence baseline.

**Why it matters:** AI-content governance (EU AI Act) leans on detection. Homogeneity means one evasion recipe defeats detection everywhere — a correlated governance failure. Cheap, fully external to labs.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind homogeneity; AI-text detection robustness literature; EU AI Act systemic-risk / transparency requirements.

# Bias Compounded: Homogeneity Turns One Model's Demographic Bias into a Society-Wide Correlated Bias

**Problem:** Failure mode A: fairness/social-bias failures. Failure mode B: inter-model homogeneity. If different providers share the same biased associations, then switching providers gives no relief, and the bias becomes a correlated, ecosystem-wide harm rather than an isolated product flaw.

**Direction:** Use an existing bias probe set (e.g., association / occupation-gender prompts). Query 6+ open models. Measure inter-model agreement on biased outputs: is the same biased completion produced across providers far more than chance? Quantify the 'no exit' effect — fraction of biased items where all providers agree.

**Why it matters:** Concentration means a shared bias is inescapable for affected groups. The compounding framing (correlation across providers, not per-model bias rate) is the novel, policy-relevant contribution and is straightforward for newcomers.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind shared blind spots; standard social-bias probes; concentration-risk framing from International AI Safety Report 2026.

# Self-Consistency Lies: Homogeneity Inflates Confidence Calibration Failures

**Problem:** Failure mode A: miscalibration / overconfidence. Failure mode B: homogeneity. Self-consistency (sample many answers, take the mode, treat agreement as confidence) assumes diverse samples. Intra-model repetition (Artificial Hivemind) means samples are not diverse, so high agreement reflects mode-collapse, not correctness — overconfidence is amplified.

**Direction:** On a QA set, sample k completions per item from open models at nonzero temperature. Measure self-consistency agreement vs actual correctness. Show that high agreement does not imply correctness for items where the model is confidently wrong, and relate the gap to the model's intra-model repetition score. Report a 'false-confidence-from-consistency' rate.

**Why it matters:** Self-consistency is a ubiquitous, cheap reliability trick used in safety-critical settings. Intra-model repetition breaks its core assumption. Quantifying when agreement is mode-collapse vs evidence is a clean, lab-independent result.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind intra-model repetition; self-consistency / calibration literature; correlated-errors (arXiv 2506.07962).

# Correlated Evaluation Gaming: Homogeneity Lets One Benchmark-Contamination Strategy Inflate All Models

**Problem:** Failure mode A: benchmark contamination / eval gaming. Failure mode B: homogeneity. If models share training data and produce homogeneous answers, contamination-driven inflation is correlated: the leaderboard looks healthy because everyone is inflated together, masking that the eval is broken.

**Direction:** Take a public benchmark with suspected contamination and a clean perturbed variant (renamed entities, reworded). Query 6+ open models on both. Measure the per-model drop AND whether drops are correlated across models (same items break for everyone). Argue that correlated drops indicate shared contamination/homogeneity rather than genuine shared capability.

**Why it matters:** Safety relies on benchmarks to track dangerous capabilities. Homogeneity-correlated contamination makes benchmarks jointly untrustworthy. A correlation analysis across models is a cheap diagnostic any outsider can run.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind homogeneity; benchmark-contamination literature; correlated-errors framing (arXiv 2506.07962).

# Benchmark Realism Gap: Synthetic vs Forum-Sourced Jailbreaks

**Problem:** A stated open problem is that jailbreak benchmarks use synthetic test cases rather than real attacker behavior; the magnitude of the gap between curated benchmark jailbreaks and jailbreaks actually shared in public attacker communities is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Collect a small corpus of publicly posted real jailbreak prompts (e.g., from public prompt-sharing sites/subreddits, fully public data) and compare their StrongREJECT-scored success and stylistic features against matched benchmark jailbreaks on the same open model. Quantify the realism gap.

**Why it matters:** Directly attacks the 'realistic jailbreak benchmarks' open problem with a measurement no lab needs proprietary data to do — using only public attacker-shared content. Establishes whether current benchmarks under- or over-estimate real-world risk, a diffuse evaluation problem.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic recommended directions list realistic jailbreak benchmarks as an open problem (subfield context). StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) and JailbreakBench (NeurIPS 2024) use curated/synthetic behaviors. The empirical gap to publicly shared real jailbreaks is unmeasured.

# Homogeneity Hides Backdoors: Shared Outputs Mask Anomaly-Based Trojan Detection

**Problem:** Failure mode A: data-poisoning / backdoors in a model. Failure mode B: homogeneity-based defenses. A proposed defense is to flag a model whose outputs diverge from peers (peer consensus as ground truth). But if a backdoor's trigger output happens to align with homogeneous peer behavior, consensus-based detection misses it; and if peers are homogeneous, a benign-but-rare correct answer looks anomalous.

**Direction:** Without training a backdoor: simulate the detection side. Take outputs from several open models plus a few 'odd-one-out' outputs (rare-correct and synthetic-trigger-like). Test whether a peer-consensus anomaly detector flags the right cases. Show false positives on rare-correct (homogeneity making correctness look anomalous) and false negatives when malicious output mimics consensus.

**Why it matters:** Cross-model consensus is a tempting cheap defense against tampered models. Homogeneity makes consensus a poor ground truth. Clarifying its failure modes is valuable safety-tooling critique, doable with inference only.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind homogeneity; correlated-errors (arXiv 2506.07962); ensemble/consensus-as-oversight assumptions (arXiv 2604.07650).

# Reasoning-Model Homogeneity: Do Chain-of-Thought Models Share the Same Reasoning Errors?

**Problem:** Failure mode A: reasoning errors / flawed CoT. Failure mode B: homogeneity, now in the reasoning trace itself. The Hivemind paper flags reasoning models as an open question. If reasoning models converge on the same flawed reasoning steps, then CoT-monitoring and cross-model reasoning checks fail correlatedly.

**Direction:** On a set of multi-step problems with known tempting-but-wrong reasoning traps, query 4-6 open reasoning-capable models. Measure homogeneity of the reasoning paths (not just answers) via step-level similarity, and whether models fall into the same trap on the same items. Report correlated-reasoning-error rates and reasoning-path homogeneity.

**Why it matters:** CoT monitoring is a leading interpretability-light oversight bet. If reasoning is homogeneous, monitoring one model's CoT generalizes its blind spots to all. Directly extends the Hivemind open problem to reasoning models, scoped to 30h.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind open question on reasoning models; correlated-errors (arXiv 2506.07962); CoT-monitoring safety literature.

# Multimodal Hivemind: Do Vision-Language Models Share Visual Blind Spots That Compound Safety Failures?

**Problem:** Failure mode A: VLM perception errors (misreading images, missing unsafe content). Failure mode B: homogeneity across VLMs. The Hivemind paper suggests testing multimodal. If VLMs share visual blind spots, content-safety pipelines that route an image past multiple VLMs fail in unison.

**Direction:** Use a small image set with known-hard or borderline-unsafe cases. Query 3-4 open VLMs for a safety-relevant judgment (e.g., 'does this image contain X'). Measure inter-model agreement on errors vs chance, and whether the same images break all models. Report correlated visual-miss rates.

**Why it matters:** Multimodal moderation is increasingly safety-critical (CSAM-adjacent, violence, deepfakes). Correlated visual blind spots mean a single evasive image type slips past all vendors. Extends Hivemind to multimodal cheaply with open VLMs.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind 'and beyond' multimodal suggestion; correlated-errors (arXiv 2506.07962); VLM safety/perception literature.

# Homogeneous Anchors: Convergent Ideation Compounds Anchoring Bias in AI-Assisted Decisions

**Problem:** Failure mode A: human over-reliance / automation bias. Failure mode B: inter-model homogeneity in brainstorming/ideation (a top Hivemind taxonomy category). If a user consults several models for options and they all converge, the user is falsely reassured ('I got a second opinion') while actually being anchored to one homogeneous answer space.

**Direction:** On Infinity-Chat brainstorm/ideation prompts, query 6+ models for option lists. Measure the union diversity of options across models vs within one model — quantify how little a 'second model' adds. Optionally a tiny human-style task: show whether the perceived-independence of multiple AIs overstates real diversity. Report a 'second-opinion value' metric.

**Why it matters:** Decision-makers treat multiple AIs as independent advisors. Homogeneity collapses that into a single voice, compounding automation bias and shrinking the option space society considers — a diffuse, long-horizon harm well-suited to outside study using the released dataset.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind ideation/brainstorm taxonomy + Infinity-Chat; automation-bias / over-reliance literature.

# Correlated Misalignment Generalization: Does Homogeneity Mean Misbehavior in One Domain Predicts It Everywhere?

**Problem:** Failure mode A: misalignment generalization (a model misbehaving in one context tends to misbehave in others). Failure mode B: homogeneity (different models share this tendency). Combined: if one widely used model shows a misaligned behavior, homogeneity implies its peers do too — correlated misalignment across the fleet.

**Direction:** Pick a small, observable proxy 'misbehavior' (e.g., willingness to give a subtly harmful tip, or to follow a manipulative system prompt). On a battery of unrelated contexts, query 6+ open models. Test (a) within-model: does misbehavior in one context predict it in others; (b) across-models: is the pattern shared. Report intra- and inter-model correlation of the misbehavior.

**Why it matters:** The International AI Safety Report flags correlated, connected safety failures. A cheap empirical demonstration that misalignment is both transferable within a model and homogeneous across models is directly on-target and needs no lab access.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind homogeneity; correlated/connected misalignment framing (International AI Safety Report 2026; arXiv 2506.07962 correlated errors).

# Homogeneity Breaks Constitutional-AI Cross-Critique: The Critic Shares the Author's Blind Spots

**Problem:** Failure mode A: harmful/flawed generation. Failure mode B: homogeneity between generator and critic in self-critique / Constitutional-AI-style revision. If the critiquing model shares the generator's blind spots, the critique step fails exactly on the harms both miss — a safety mechanism nullified by homogeneity.

**Direction:** Generate borderline outputs with model A, then have models B,C,D (varying homogeneity to A) critique/revise them against a fixed rubric. Measure catch-rate of injected flaws as a function of generator-critic output similarity. Show catch-rate drops as homogeneity rises; identify which harm categories are jointly missed.

**Why it matters:** Self-critique and AI-feedback are cornerstone alignment techniques. Quantifying that a homogeneous critic adds little safety value (and which harms slip through) is a practical, lab-independent contribution to oversight design.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind shared blind spots; Constitutional AI / self-critique literature; correlated errors (arXiv 2506.07962).

# Concentration Plus Drift: How Provider Monoculture Turns a Silent Model Update into a Correlated Regression

**Problem:** Failure mode A: silent model updates / behavioral drift breaking downstream systems. Failure mode B: provider concentration (homogeneity-driven dependence on few models). When many systems depend on the same model, one update is a correlated, simultaneous regression across all of them.

**Direction:** Using two snapshots/versions of available open models (or two checkpoints), build a small suite of downstream 'contracts' (format, refusal boundary, factual answers). Measure how many contracts break per version change, and simulate fleet impact: if N systems share the model, one update breaks correlated subsets. Produce a 'blast radius of an update' estimate tied to concentration.

**Why it matters:** The International AI Safety Report highlights cascading failures from shared-provider dependence. A concrete, measured demonstration of correlated regression risk from a single update is a tangible systemic-risk contribution feasible with open checkpoints.

**Relevant context:** International AI Safety Report 2026 cascading/concentration risk; Artificial Hivemind homogeneity; behavioral-drift literature.

# Homogeneity Amplifies Data-Voids: Shared Failure on Low-Resource Languages Compounds Mistranslation Harms

**Problem:** Failure mode A: poor performance / unsafe behavior on low-resource languages. Failure mode B: homogeneity. If all providers share the same low-resource blind spot, a safety-critical mistranslation (medical, legal) fails identically across every provider — no fallback exists.

**Direction:** Pick a low-resource language and a small set of safety-sensitive prompts (with verified reference answers). Query 5-6 open multilingual models. Measure inter-model agreement on errors and whether the same items fail across all models (correlated low-resource failure) vs a high-resource control. Report the 'no safe provider' rate.

**Why it matters:** Concentration means underserved-language communities face a correlated, inescapable safety gap. The correlation framing (not per-model accuracy) is novel and policy-relevant; fully doable by outside researchers with open models.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind shared blind spots; multilingual-LLM safety/quality literature; concentration risk (International AI Safety Report 2026).

# Homogeneity Defeats Red-Team Diversity: One Attacker Model Covers the Same Ground as Many

**Problem:** Failure mode A: incomplete red-teaming (attacks miss whole regions of failure space). Failure mode B: homogeneity among attacker models. Automated red-teaming uses LLMs to generate attacks; if attacker models are homogeneous, using several of them explores barely more than one — red-team coverage is correlatedly limited.

**Direction:** Have 5-6 open models each generate adversarial prompts for a fixed target behavior. Measure the diversity/coverage of the union of attacks vs a single model's set (semantic clustering of attacks). Quantify marginal coverage added per extra attacker model and relate it to attacker-model homogeneity. Report a 'red-team diversity ceiling'.

**Why it matters:** Automated red-teaming is a key pre-deployment safety practice. If attacker homogeneity caps coverage, dangerous failure regions go untested everywhere. Measuring the coverage ceiling is a cheap, infrastructure-building contribution outsiders can own.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind intra/inter-model homogeneity; automated red-teaming literature; diversity-metric methods (LLM-TOPLA, arXiv 2410.03953).

# Correlated Tool-Misuse: Homogeneous Agents Make the Same Dangerous API Call on the Same Triggers

**Problem:** Failure mode A: unsafe tool/function-calling decisions by agents (e.g., over-eagerly executing a destructive action). Failure mode B: homogeneity. If different model-backed agents share the same unsafe tool-use disposition, a single triggering situation causes correlated unsafe actions across an ecosystem of agents.

**Direction:** Build a minimal sandboxed tool-use harness with a clearly-unsafe option (e.g., 'delete_all' vs 'confirm'). Present borderline scenarios to 5-6 open models acting as agents. Measure per-model unsafe-action rate AND inter-model correlation: do the same scenarios trigger unsafe actions across models? Report correlated-unsafe-action rates vs independence.

**Why it matters:** Multi-agent ecosystems on homogeneous models could take simultaneous unsafe actions — a concrete systemic-risk scenario. A small sandbox prototype doubles as reusable monitoring infrastructure, exactly the kind of counterfactually valuable work outsiders can build.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind homogeneity; correlated-errors (arXiv 2506.07962); agentic tool-use safety literature; International AI Safety Report 2026 cascading failures.

# Harmful-Quality Ceiling: When Jailbroken Models Hallucinate Danger

**Problem:** Concern about jailbreaks assumes harmful outputs are accurate; but if jailbroken models frequently produce confidently wrong harmful content (e.g., incorrect synthesis steps), the genuine uplift is overstated, and this accuracy dimension is rarely measured.

**Direction:** For a set of verifiable borderline-harmful tasks (e.g., basic chemistry/biology facts with known ground truth, security trivia), jailbreak an open model and score not just willingness but factual accuracy of the harmful content against ground truth. Report a willingness-vs-accuracy breakdown.

**Why it matters:** Reframes uplift assessment around accuracy, a neglected, fuzzy-reward dimension central to whether jailbreaks pose real-world danger. Uses only public factual ground truth and an open model — strongly counterfactual and feasible, with clear success criteria.

**Relevant context:** StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) found jailbreaks reduce capability; uplift debates (e.g., bio/chem) hinge on accuracy. Measuring factual accuracy of jailbroken harmful outputs against verifiable ground truth as a robustness dimension is largely unexplored.

# Persuasion Monoculture: Homogeneous Outputs Make AI-Driven Manipulation Correlated and Hard to Inoculate

**Problem:** Failure mode A: AI persuasion/manipulation. Failure mode B: homogeneity. If models converge on the same persuasive framings and arguments, then at scale the population is exposed to a narrow, correlated set of manipulative patterns — and defenses tuned to one model's style fail against all because the style is shared.

**Direction:** On persuasion-style Infinity-Chat prompts (argue for X), query 6+ models and measure homogeneity of the rhetorical strategies/arguments produced (cluster arguments, measure overlap). Then test whether a simple 'argument-pattern' detector trained on one model's outputs transfers to others (it should, if homogeneous). Report homogeneity of persuasion and detector transfer.

**Why it matters:** Mass persuasion via homogeneous AI is a medium-horizon societal risk. Homogeneity is a double-edged sword here (easier to detect but more correlated exposure); quantifying both effects with the released dataset is novel and lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** Artificial Hivemind homogeneity + Infinity-Chat persuasion-relevant categories; AI-persuasion/manipulation literature; AI-text detection transfer.

# Do Models Share Safety Blind Spots? Extending Correlated Errors to Refusal Decisions

**Problem:** Kim et al. (Correlated Errors in LLMs) show 350+ models make correlated mistakes on factual benchmarks, driven by shared providers/architecture. But they never test whether SAFETY decisions (refuse vs. comply on borderline-harmful prompts) are correlated. If models share blind spots on which requests are dangerous, a single jailbreak class could slip past many deployed safety filters at once.

**Direction:** Take ~15-20 open and API-accessible models from different providers. Run them on a few hundred borderline/ambiguous safety prompts (mix of clearly-harmful, clearly-benign, and genuinely-ambiguous). Record refuse/comply for each. Compute pairwise error-correlation (where 'error' = disagreement with a majority-vote or a small human-labeled gold set) and compare against the independent-decisions baseline used by Kim et al. Break down correlation by provider family.

**Why it matters:** Correlated safety blind spots are a systemic risk: if the same ambiguous-but-harmful prompts sail past most filters, defense-in-depth via 'use several models' is illusory. This is exactly the diffuse, fuzzy-reward evaluation that needs no lab infrastructure and is high counterfactual value outside a frontier lab.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Correlated Errors in Large Language Models' (Kim et al., arXiv:2506.07962, June 2025), which found 60% agreement when both models err and stronger correlation within provider families, but focused on factual/leaderboard tasks not safety refusals.

# Is the Hivemind Worse on Safety-Relevant Open-Ended Queries?

**Problem:** The Artificial Hivemind paper documents intra- and inter-model homogeneity on general open-ended queries via Infinity-Chat, but does not isolate safety-relevant prompts (e.g., 'how should I think about whether to report a coworker', 'what are risks of X technology'). If homogeneity is even stronger on these, the public gets a narrowed, single-perspective view of high-stakes questions.

**Direction:** Filter or hand-curate a few hundred safety/ethics/risk-framing open-ended prompts. Sample N completions per model across ~8 models. Reuse the paper's homogeneity metrics (semantic embedding similarity within and across models) and compare safety-relevant vs. matched neutral prompts. Test whether convergence on a single recommended framing is higher for safety topics.

**Why it matters:** If models converge to one dominant framing of risk/ethics questions, society loses the diversity of perspectives needed to spot AI risks — a slow, diffuse, >1-year threat model labs deprioritize. Pure inference + open benchmark, no training.

**Relevant context:** Directly extends 'Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond)' (Jiang et al., arXiv:2510.22954, Oct 2025, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper) and its Infinity-Chat dataset to the untested safety-relevant slice flagged in the paper's own future-work.

# Does Verbalized Sampling Reduce Cross-Model Homogeneity, or Just Within-Model?

**Problem:** Verbalized Sampling (VS) mitigates within-model mode collapse by prompting a model to verbalize a distribution over responses. It was evaluated per-model. Unknown: does VS make DIFFERENT models diverge from each other, or do they all collapse to the same enriched set? If VS-diversified outputs across models are still mutually similar, the systemic homogeneity problem remains unsolved.

**Direction:** Apply the VS prompt template to ~6 models on a shared set of open-ended prompts. Compare cross-model output similarity (embedding-based) under standard prompting vs. VS. Test whether VS increases intra-model diversity but leaves inter-model homogeneity intact — the key distinction the original paper didn't measure.

**Why it matters:** Cheap inference-time fixes are appealing precisely because they need no lab resources. Showing whether they address SYSTEMIC (cross-model) homogeneity vs. only local diversity tells the field whether prompting alone can buy diversity insurance.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Verbalized Sampling: How to Mitigate Mode Collapse and Unlock LLM Diversity' (Zhang et al., arXiv:2510.01171, Oct 2025), which measured within-model diversity only; combines with cross-model homogeneity metrics from Artificial Hivemind (arXiv:2510.22954).

# Replicating Algorithmic Monoculture in Hiring with Open LLM Resume Screeners

**Problem:** Bommasani et al. (Algorithmic Monocultures in Hiring) found correlated, homogeneous rejection outcomes when one vendor screens many applicants — using proprietary pymetrics data unavailable to outside researchers. The LLM analogue (many firms using GPT/Claude/Llama to screen resumes) is exactly what an independent researcher can test with synthetic resumes.

**Direction:** Generate a synthetic but realistic pool of ~200 resumes across demographics/skill profiles. Have ~6 LLMs each score/rank them for a few job descriptions. Measure systemic rejection rate (fraction of candidates rejected by ALL models) vs. an independent-decisions null, and test for demographic disparity in homogeneous rejections. Mirror the paper's outcome-homogenization metric.

**Why it matters:** Replicating a proprietary-data finding with fully open, synthetic data is high counterfactual value: it lets the public audit a real allocational harm (being locked out of all jobs at once) without lab/vendor access. Medium-horizon societal risk.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Algorithmic Monocultures in Hiring' (Bommasani et al., arXiv:2605.27371, FAccT 2026, June 2026) from a single proprietary vendor to publicly-accessible LLM screeners; builds on outcome-homogenization framing.

# Do LLM Judges From the Same Family Form a Correlated-Error Monoculture?

**Problem:** Multi-agent-judge and ensemble-judge papers assume that using several LLM judges reduces bias. But recent work warns that if judges share a base model they share blind spots. No one has quantified, on a shared evaluation set, how much error-correlation persists across judge models from the same vs. different families.

**Direction:** Build a small set of responses with known quality labels (or strong human/gold judgments). Have ~8 LLM judges score them. Compute inter-judge error correlation, grouped by provider family. Test whether an ensemble of same-family judges gives near-zero effective diversity (correlated errors) vs. cross-family ensembles. Estimate effective number of independent judges.

**Why it matters:** LLM-as-judge is becoming the backbone of automated safety evals. If judge ensembles are a monoculture, our evaluation infrastructure has correlated blind spots — a foundational, infrastructure-level safety concern doable without lab access.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Correlated Errors in Large Language Models' (arXiv:2506.07962) and 'Multi-Agent Debate for LLM Judges with Adaptive Stability Detection' (arXiv:2510.12697, Oct 2025), which note correlated-error risk for judges but do not quantify effective judge diversity.

# Jailbreak Transfer as a Homogeneity Thermometer Across Open Models

**Problem:** Angell et al. show jailbreak transferability emerges from shared representations: more representationally similar models inherit each other's jailbreaks. This gives a concrete, behavioral proxy for dangerous homogeneity, but the relationship hasn't been turned into a cheap diagnostic an outside auditor could use to flag at-risk model pairs.

**Direction:** Take ~8-10 open-weight models and a handful of public jailbreak prompts. Measure (a) pairwise jailbreak transfer rate and (b) a cheap representational-similarity proxy (e.g., cosine similarity of hidden states or even output-distribution similarity on benign prompts). Test how well the cheap proxy predicts transfer, building a 'homogeneity risk map' of which model pairs share attack surface.

**Why it matters:** A lightweight, weights-light diagnostic for shared attack surface lets independent auditors warn when deploying multiple 'diverse' models gives no real defense-in-depth. Directly safety-relevant and infrastructure-flavored.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations' (Angell et al., arXiv:2506.12913, June 2025, ICLR 2026) by turning its representational-similarity finding into a practical auditing diagnostic.

# Quantifying the Effective Number of Independent Foundation Models in Practice

**Problem:** The 'Quantifying Systemic Vulnerability in the Foundation Model Industry' paper assesses concentration via inputs (compute, energy, talent). It does not measure BEHAVIORAL concentration: even if there were 50 model providers, if their outputs cluster into 3 behavioral types, effective diversity is ~3. No simple behavioral diversity index exists.

**Direction:** Run ~20 accessible models on a fixed battery of prompts (factual, refusal, open-ended). Build a behavioral fingerprint per model (agreement vectors / output embeddings). Cluster and compute an 'effective number of independent models' (e.g., via eigenvalue participation ratio of the agreement matrix). Compare to the count of nominal providers.

**Why it matters:** Concentration risk policy (EU AI Act systemic-risk) needs a measurable behavioral diversity index, not just input counts. A reproducible, infrastructure-level metric anyone can compute is exactly counterfactually valuable for systemic-risk monitoring.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Quantifying Systemic Vulnerability in the Foundation Model Industry' (arXiv:2510.23421, Oct 2025) from input-concentration to behavioral-concentration metrics, using correlated-error methodology from arXiv:2506.07962.

# Do Reasoning Models Actually Reduce Inter-Model Homogeneity?

**Problem:** 'Reasoning Models Generate Societies of Thought' claims reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, QwQ) show greater perspective diversity than instruction-tuned models. But that was measured WITHIN models. Whether reasoning models DIVERGE from one another (lower cross-model homogeneity) on open-ended/safety queries is untested — and matters for whether 'just use reasoning models' buys systemic diversity.

**Direction:** Compare a set of reasoning models vs. matched instruction-tuned models on shared open-ended prompts. Use Artificial Hivemind-style cross-model similarity metrics. Test whether final answers (not just CoT) of reasoning models are less mutually similar, or whether their reasoning still converges to the same conclusions.

**Why it matters:** If reasoning models converge to identical conclusions despite diverse CoT, the apparent diversity is cosmetic and systemic blind-spot risk persists. Cheap inference experiment with clear safety framing.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Reasoning Models Generate Societies of Thought' (arXiv:2601.10825, Jan 2026) by testing CROSS-model rather than within-model diversity, evaluated with Artificial Hivemind metrics (arXiv:2510.22954).

# Format-Induced Diversity Collapse on Safety-Relevant Prompts

**Problem:** 'The Price of Format: Diversity Collapse in LLMs' shows structured output formats (JSON, multiple-choice) collapse response diversity. Unstudied: whether forcing structured formats on safety/risk-assessment prompts makes multiple models collapse to the SAME answer, amplifying systemic homogeneity exactly when diverse risk assessments are most needed.

**Direction:** Take safety/risk-assessment prompts (e.g., 'rate the danger of this scenario', 'list risks of plan X'). Compare free-form vs. JSON/structured outputs across ~6 models. Measure both within-model diversity drop and cross-model convergence under structured formats.

**Why it matters:** Production AI systems force structured outputs for tooling. If this silently homogenizes safety judgments across an ecosystem, it's a hidden systemic risk introduced by engineering convenience — auditable with pure inference.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'The Price of Format: Diversity Collapse in LLMs' (arXiv:2505.18949, May 2025) to safety-relevant prompts and to the cross-model homogeneity dimension.

# Defense Stacking Interference: Do Two Cheap Defenses Conflict?

**Problem:** Defenders deploy multiple cheap defenses (perplexity filter + activation probe + system-prompt reminder), but whether combining them produces additive robustness, redundant cost, or harmful interference (e.g., compounded over-refusal) is not characterized for accessible setups.

**Direction:** Implement 2-3 lightweight defenses around one open model and evaluate every combination on a small jailbreak suite and an over-refusal suite, measuring marginal robustness gain and marginal over-refusal cost per added defense. Identify whether stacking has diminishing or negative returns.

**Why it matters:** Real deployments stack defenses, yet the cost-constrained-monitor question (which combination is Pareto-optimal) is understudied for small actors. A reproducible stacking ablation is cheap infrastructure-light research with direct deployment relevance.

**Relevant context:** Combining Cost-Constrained Runtime Monitors for AI Safety (arXiv:2507.15886) studies monitor combination; XSTest/OR-Bench measure over-refusal cost. A concrete, reproducible stacking ablation of cheap defenses on an open model with both robustness and over-refusal axes is missing.

# Are LLM Red-Teamers a Monoculture? Measuring Attack Homogeneity Across Attacker Models

**Problem:** The Quality-Diversity Evolution paper notes LLM-as-attacker methods suffer mode collapse: attackers generate similar prompts and miss diverse failure modes. They fix it within one attacker. Untested: how homogeneous are attacks ACROSS different attacker models? If all attacker LLMs probe the same regions, automated red-teaming has shared blind spots.

**Direction:** Have ~5 attacker LLMs each generate adversarial prompts against a fixed target. Embed and cluster the generated attacks. Measure cross-attacker coverage overlap and the union vs. intersection of failure modes discovered. Quantify how much marginal coverage each additional attacker family adds.

**Why it matters:** If our automated red-teaming tools are a monoculture, vulnerabilities they all miss are systematically unaudited — a direct safety-tooling blind spot. Infrastructure-relevant, no training, single GPU for open targets.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Quality-Diversity Evolution for Discovering Diverse Vulnerabilities in LLM Safety' (arXiv:2606.00801, June 2026) from intra-attacker to inter-attacker diversity of discovered failure modes.

# Does Distillation Inherit the Teacher's Homogeneity AND Blind Spots? A Small-Scale Audit

**Problem:** Angell et al. show benign-only distillation toward a teacher increases representational similarity and inherits the teacher's jailbreak vulnerabilities. The broader homogeneity implication — that the proliferation of distilled small models recreates the teacher's blind spots ecosystem-wide — hasn't been audited behaviorally on publicly available teacher/student pairs.

**Direction:** Pick public teacher/student pairs (e.g., a large model and its known distilled variants/families). Without any training, behaviorally compare them: agreement on factual errors, refusal patterns, and shared jailbreak susceptibility. Test whether distilled students cluster tightly around their teacher, forming homogeneity families.

**Why it matters:** If thousands of cheap distilled models all carry one teacher's blind spots, the apparent diversity of the open-model ecosystem is illusory — a key systemic concentration risk. Pure behavioral audit, no training, counterfactually valuable outside labs.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations' (arXiv:2506.12913, June 2025) using only behavioral probing of existing public teacher/student model families.

# Universal Embedding Geometry as a Single Point of Failure for RAG Safety Filters

**Problem:** 'Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings' shows different embedding models share a universal latent geometry (translatable without paired data). Implication for safety: if an embedding-based safety filter (e.g., a retrieval/refusal classifier) has a blind spot, that blind spot may transfer across all embedding models because they share geometry — making 'switch embedding model' no defense.

**Direction:** Build a simple embedding-based content filter (nearest-neighbor to known-harmful examples) using ~4 different open embedding models. Find inputs that evade one filter and test whether the SAME evasions transfer across embedding models. Correlate transfer with embedding-similarity, testing the shared-geometry blind-spot hypothesis.

**Why it matters:** RAG and embedding filters are everywhere in deployed safety stacks. If their blind spots are universal due to shared geometry, embedding diversity is a false safeguard — an infrastructure-level systemic risk testable on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings' (arXiv:2505.12540, May 2025, latest v4 Jan 2026) to the safety-filter-evasion-transfer setting.

# Homogenization in Synthetic Training Data: Does Model-Generated Data Narrow the Next Generation?

**Problem:** Verbalized Sampling and the Hivemind paper both flag synthetic-data contamination as a homogeneity driver. But the concrete claim — that using one model's synthetic outputs as data narrows the diversity available downstream — is rarely measured directly with simple diversity metrics on the data itself (no retraining needed).

**Direction:** Have several models generate synthetic datasets for the same task (e.g., paraphrases, QA pairs, instruction-response). Measure lexical/semantic diversity within each model's synthetic set and overlap across models. Compare to human-written reference data. Quantify how much diversity is lost relative to the human distribution — a data-level homogeneity audit.

**Why it matters:** As the web fills with synthetic text and labs train on it, an ecosystem-wide diversity collapse (model autophagy) is a medium-horizon systemic risk. Measuring it at the data level needs no training and no lab data.

**Relevant context:** Extends mechanisms identified in 'Artificial Hivemind' (arXiv:2510.22954) and 'Verbalized Sampling' (arXiv:2510.01171) by measuring diversity loss directly in model-generated synthetic data.

# Multi-Agent Workflows Are Homogeneous: Measuring Correlated Failure in Same-Base-Model Agent Systems

**Problem:** 'Rethinking the Value of Multi-Agent Workflow' observes most agent frameworks are homogeneous (agents share one base LLM, differ only by prompts/tools). If agents in a 'check each other' workflow share blind spots, the safety promise of multi-agent oversight collapses under correlated mistakes — but this correlation hasn't been measured on safety-monitoring tasks.

**Direction:** Set up a simple multi-agent monitor (one agent acts, others review) all using the same base model, vs. a heterogeneous version mixing model families. On a set of tasks with injected errors/unsafe actions, measure whether same-base-model reviewers catch fewer injected problems (correlated blind spots) than cross-family reviewers. Report detection rate vs. agent diversity.

**Why it matters:** Scalable oversight increasingly relies on agents monitoring agents. If homogeneous agent stacks share blind spots, oversight is weaker than assumed — a core safety-tooling result, prototypable on one GPU with open models.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Rethinking the Value of Multi-Agent Workflow: A Strong Single Agent Baseline' (arXiv:2601.12307, Jan 2026) and correlated-error findings (arXiv:2506.07962) to safety-monitoring tasks.

# Majority Vote vs. Correlated Mistakes: When Ensembling Same-Family Models Backfires on Safety

**Problem:** 'Auditing Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning Trees' notes majority voting fails under correlated mistakes. The community keeps using vote/ensemble for safety-critical decisions assuming independence. The conditions under which same-family ensembling actively HURTS (confidently wrong consensus) on safety judgments aren't characterized for non-experts.

**Direction:** On a labeled set of safety judgments (harmful/benign, policy violations), compare single-model accuracy vs. majority vote over (a) same-family models and (b) cross-family models. Identify cases where same-family majority vote is confidently wrong because all members share the error. Quantify the 'false confidence from correlated votes' rate.

**Why it matters:** Voting/ensembling is the most common cheap robustness trick. Showing it can amplify rather than reduce correlated safety errors is directly actionable and needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Auditing Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning Trees Outperforms Majority Vote and LLM-as-Judge' (arXiv:2602.09341, Feb 2026) and correlated-error work (arXiv:2506.07962) to safety-decision aggregation.

# Mapping Shared Blind Spots: What Do ALL Models Get Wrong Together?

**Problem:** Kim et al. show error correlation but don't characterize the CONTENT of universally-shared errors. Knowing WHICH categories of questions every model fails on simultaneously (the 'collective blind spot map') is more actionable for safety than an aggregate correlation number — and no such public map exists.

**Direction:** Run ~15 models across a broad, categorized benchmark (factual, reasoning, safety-judgment). Identify items where ALL or nearly-all models err. Cluster these universal-failure items by topic/type to produce a taxonomy of collective blind spots. Analyze whether they concentrate in specific domains (e.g., niche cultures, recent events, certain risk types).

**Why it matters:** A public 'collective blind spot map' tells deployers where NO current model can be trusted and where human oversight is non-negotiable — diffuse, fuzzy-reward, high counterfactual value, doable with pure inference.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Correlated Errors in Large Language Models' (arXiv:2506.07962, June 2025) from aggregate correlation statistics to a categorized taxonomy of universally-shared failures.

# Does Homogeneity Increase With Model Capability? A Capability-Stratified Audit

**Problem:** Kim et al. report the surprising result that larger, more accurate models have MORE correlated errors, even across providers. If true broadly, scaling makes the ecosystem MORE of a monoculture — the opposite of the usual 'diversity will save us' assumption. This capability-vs-homogeneity trend deserves a focused, replicable audit on open-ended and safety tasks, not just leaderboards.

**Direction:** Stratify ~15 accessible models into capability tiers (small/mid/frontier). Measure within-tier and cross-tier output homogeneity on open-ended and safety prompts. Test whether higher-capability tiers are MORE mutually similar. Visualize the homogeneity-vs-capability trend.

**Why it matters:** If capability and homogeneity rise together, future frontier ecosystems are inherently more concentrated and fragile — a >1-year systemic threat model labs underweight. Replicable with pure inference.

**Relevant context:** Extends the 'larger/more accurate models have more correlated errors' finding from 'Correlated Errors in LLMs' (arXiv:2506.07962) to open-ended/safety tasks and a capability-stratified design.

# Cross-Model Convergence on Moral Dilemmas: A Hivemind Audit of Value Pluralism

**Problem:** Infinity-Chat shows models, reward models, and judges are poorly calibrated to idiosyncratic human preferences. A sharp, safety-relevant slice — moral/value-laden dilemmas with legitimately diverse human answers — hasn't been audited for whether models collapse to a single 'house view' that overrides human value pluralism.

**Direction:** Curate value-laden dilemmas with documented human disagreement (e.g., trolley variants, fairness-vs-liberty tradeoffs, contested policy questions). Sample many completions across ~8 models. Measure cross-model convergence to a dominant answer and compare against the spread of human opinion. Quantify how much value pluralism is lost.

**Why it matters:** If a few models impose a single moral framing at societal scale, that's a slow, diffuse value-lock-in risk — exactly the long-horizon, hard-to-measure problem labs deprioritize. Pure inference, open data.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Artificial Hivemind' (arXiv:2510.22954, NeurIPS 2025) and its Infinity-Chat finding on idiosyncratic-preference miscalibration to value-laden moral dilemmas.

# Temperature and Sampling: Can Decoding Tricks Break Cross-Model Homogeneity?

**Problem:** The Hivemind paper attributes homogeneity to data/alignment, implying decoding tricks won't fix it. Verbalized Sampling suggests prompting can. Nobody has cleanly tested whether simple, free decoding interventions (high temperature, nucleus, diverse beam, min-p) reduce CROSS-model homogeneity vs. just adding noise within a model.

**Direction:** On shared open-ended prompts, sweep decoding parameters across ~6 models. Measure within-model diversity and cross-model similarity at each setting. Test whether any decoding regime makes models genuinely diverge (cover different semantic regions) vs. all just getting noisier around the same mode.

**Why it matters:** If the cheapest possible fix (turn up temperature) can't buy systemic diversity, it sharpens the case that homogeneity is baked into training — informing whether structural interventions are required. Trivial compute, pure inference.

**Relevant context:** Tests competing claims in 'Artificial Hivemind' (arXiv:2510.22954) vs. 'Verbalized Sampling' (arXiv:2510.01171) and 'The Price of Format' (arXiv:2505.18949) about whether inference-time changes affect homogeneity.

# Prefill-Recovery as a Behavioral Fingerprint for Hidden Misalignment

**Problem:** A model that complies harmfully only after a prefill but verbalizes nothing suspicious is a model-organism for non-verbalized misalignment; the prefill-recovery profile could serve as a behavioral fingerprint, but this framing has not been tested.

**Direction:** Treat prefill-recovery curves as behavioral fingerprints and test whether a deliberately abliterated (refusal-removed) open model versus its aligned base produces distinguishable fingerprints, even when surface refusals look similar. Assess whether the fingerprint detects 'silent' alignment removal.

**Why it matters:** Probes a model-organism question (detecting a model that misbehaves without verbalizing it) using only behavioral inference, no internal lab tooling. If prefill fingerprints reveal hidden tampering, it is a cheap auditing technique for open-weight supply-chain safety — a medium-horizon concern.

**Relevant context:** Abliteration removes refusal while preserving capabilities (Arditi et al., NeurIPS 2024; arXiv:2509.15202). Open-weight fine-tuning defenses are easily stripped (arXiv:2605.26526). Using prefill-recovery behavior as a tamper/fingerprint detector for silently de-aligned models is an untested framing.

# Provider-Family Fingerprinting: Can You Identify a Model's Lineage From Its Errors?

**Problem:** Kim et al. find error correlation is driven partly by shared provider. Flipping this: if models within a provider family share a distinctive error signature, you should be able to fingerprint a black-box model's lineage from its mistakes alone. This is an untested, practically useful consequence of homogeneity for transparency/auditing.

**Direction:** Collect error/refusal patterns of ~15 models on a fixed probe set. Train a simple classifier (logistic regression on agreement features) to predict provider family from behavioral fingerprint. Evaluate accuracy and which probes are most lineage-revealing. This reveals how much hidden homogeneity exists within families.

**Why it matters:** Lineage fingerprinting supports supply-chain transparency (detecting undisclosed reliance on one base model) — a concentration-risk monitoring tool deployable by outsiders. Simple stats/ML, fits participant skill set.

**Relevant context:** Extends the provider-driven correlation finding in 'Correlated Errors in Large Language Models' (arXiv:2506.07962, June 2025) into a behavioral lineage-fingerprinting task.

# Does Multi-Agent Debate Homogenize or Diversify? Tracking Disagreement Decay

**Problem:** 'Talk Isn't Always Cheap' finds agent disagreement DECREASES as debate progresses and correlates with performance degradation. The safety implication — that debate, intended to surface diverse views, actually drives agents toward premature consensus (homogenization-by-conversation) — needs a focused, replicable measurement, especially for safety judgments.

**Direction:** Run multi-round debates between LLM agents on contested safety/factual questions. At each round, measure inter-agent disagreement and distance to the final consensus. Quantify how fast diversity collapses and whether the collapse is toward correct or incorrect answers. Compare same-family vs. cross-family debater pools.

**Why it matters:** Debate is a proposed scalable-oversight mechanism. If it homogenizes agents into confident consensus (right or wrong), it can manufacture false agreement — a subtle oversight failure mode, prototypable on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate' (arXiv:2509.05396, Sept 2025) by framing disagreement decay as a homogenization process and adding the same/cross-family comparison.

# Homogeneity of Omission: Do Models Share the Same Blind Spots in What They DON'T Say?

**Problem:** 'Biases in the Blind Spot: Detecting What LLMs Fail to Mention' studies what a single model omits. The systemic question — whether different models OMIT the same considerations (shared blind spots of omission) — is untested. If all models silently skip the same caveats/risks, the public is uniformly under-informed.

**Direction:** On prompts that should elicit caveats (e.g., 'is plan X safe?', 'what could go wrong with Y?'), collect ~8 models' responses. Build a reference checklist of relevant considerations (from a strong model or light human input). Measure which considerations are omitted by ALL models — the shared omission blind spots — vs. model-specific omissions.

**Why it matters:** Shared omissions are invisible failures: nobody sees the missing caveat because every model omits it. Mapping them is high-value, diffuse safety work needing only inference and light annotation.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Biases in the Blind Spot: Detecting What LLMs Fail to Mention' (arXiv:2602.10117, Feb 2026) from single-model omissions to cross-model shared omissions.

# Cascading Hallucination: Do Homogeneous Models Reinforce Each Other's Errors in Pipelines?

**Problem:** Concentration-risk reports warn about cascading failures when systems depend on the same model. A concrete, testable micro-version: in a pipeline where one model's output feeds another (summarize-then-answer, generate-then-verify), do homogeneous models fail to catch each other's hallucinations because they share the blind spot, while heterogeneous pairs catch more?

**Direction:** Build a two-stage pipeline (generator -> verifier). On a set of prompts with known-correct answers, inject the generator's natural hallucinations and measure verifier catch-rate when verifier is same-family vs. different-family from the generator. Quantify the cascade-amplification effect of homogeneity.

**Why it matters:** Production AI pipelines chain models, often from one provider. Demonstrating that homogeneity lets errors cascade uncaught is a concrete, infrastructure-relevant systemic-risk result, fully reproducible with open models on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Operationalizes cascading-failure concerns from the International AI Safety Report 2026 and 'Quantifying Systemic Vulnerability in the Foundation Model Industry' (arXiv:2510.23421) at the pipeline level, using correlated-error methodology (arXiv:2506.07962).

# Quantifying Homogenization of Human Writing After LLM Assistance

**Problem:** 'The Homogenizing Effect of LLMs on Human Expression and Thought' argues conceptually that LLMs narrow human expression. A small empirical test — measuring whether human writing becomes more mutually similar after LLM editing assistance, and whether different LLM assistants push toward the SAME style — is feasible and underexplored.

**Direction:** Take a corpus of diverse human-written short texts. Have ~4 different LLMs 'improve/polish' each. Measure diversity (lexical, syntactic, semantic) before vs. after, and whether outputs of different LLM assistants converge to a shared style. Quantify the homogenizing pull of LLM assistance and its cross-assistant consistency.

**Why it matters:** Ecosystem-wide flattening of human expression and thought is a slow, civilizational-scale risk frontier labs won't prioritize. A clean empirical demonstration with open data is high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'The Homogenizing Effect of Large Language Models on Human Expression and Thought' (arXiv:2508.01491, Aug 2025) from conceptual argument to a small empirical before/after measurement.

# Mode Collapse Toward the Majority: Auditing Minority-Perspective Suppression Across Models

**Problem:** 'The Homogenization Problem in LLMs' argues mode collapse concentrates on dominant modes and attenuates minoritized ones, and that it's baked into post-training (not fixable at inference). A cross-model audit measuring whether MULTIPLE models suppress the SAME minority perspectives/representations identically would quantify the systemic dimension.

**Direction:** Use prompts known to surface representational diversity (occupations, family structures, cultural practices, contested viewpoints). Sample many completions across ~6 models. Measure how often each model surfaces minority modes and whether the SAME modes are suppressed across all models (shared suppression) vs. model-specific. Compare to a real-world reference distribution where available.

**Why it matters:** If all models erase the same minorities identically, the harm is systemic and invisible — no single-model audit reveals it. Quantifying shared suppression is exactly the diffuse, fuzzy-reward safety work that needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'The Homogenization Problem in LLMs: Towards Meaningful Diversity in AI Safety' (arXiv:2601.06116, Jan 2026) to a cross-model SHARED-suppression measurement.

# A Lightweight Homogeneity Monitor: Prototype Dashboard for Systemic Output Convergence

**Problem:** Open problems list calls for monitoring approaches for systemic/concentration risk spanning multiple deployed systems, but no simple, runnable monitoring prototype exists for outsiders. EU AI Act systemic-risk monitoring needs tools, yet current work is descriptive (vulnerability indices) rather than operational.

**Direction:** Build a small reproducible harness: feed a fixed daily/periodic prompt battery to N accessible models, compute a single cross-model homogeneity index (mean pairwise output similarity + effective-number-of-models) and plot it over models/time. Validate it tracks known same-family clustering. Ship it as a tiny open tool plus a blog post on what it reveals.

**Why it matters:** Strategically valuable infrastructure: a public, low-cost homogeneity monitor lets regulators, deployers, and researchers track systemic convergence risk without lab access — directly serving the concentration-risk monitoring open problem.

**Relevant context:** Operationalizes monitoring needs from the International AI Safety Report 2026 and EU AI Act systemic-risk requirements, using metrics from 'Quantifying Systemic Vulnerability' (arXiv:2510.23421) and 'Correlated Errors' (arXiv:2506.07962).

# Does PRISM-Style Pluralistic Prompting Reduce Cross-Model Homogeneity?

**Problem:** PRISM (Pluralistic Reasoning via In-context Structure Modeling) targets pluralistic reasoning within a model. Whether an in-context pluralism intervention applied across DIFFERENT models makes them diverge (cover different perspectives) rather than each independently listing the same canned 'multiple perspectives' is untested and matters for systemic diversity.

**Direction:** Apply a PRISM-style pluralistic prompt across ~6 models on contested prompts. Compare cross-model coverage of distinct perspectives vs. baseline prompting. Test whether models still converge on the SAME enumerated perspectives (cosmetic pluralism) or genuinely cover complementary regions, measured by union/overlap of perspective clusters.

**Why it matters:** Clarifies whether prompt-level pluralism interventions address systemic homogeneity or just produce identical 'on-one-hand/on-the-other' templates everywhere — a cheap inference experiment with clear safety framing.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Shared Nature, Unique Nurture: PRISM for Pluralistic Reasoning via In-context Structure Modeling' (arXiv:2602.21317, Feb 2026) to the cross-model homogeneity setting.

# Do Steering Vectors Survive a Jailbreak? Measuring Refusal-Vector Neutralization Under Adversarial Prefixes

**Problem:** Concept-vector steering is proposed as a safety lever, but it is unknown whether an attacker who controls the prompt can craft inputs that quietly cancel a deployed steering vector. The open-problem list in the subfield context explicitly flags adversarial robustness of concept vectors as unresolved.

**Direction:** On an open model (Llama-3.1-8B or Gemma-2-9B), extract a 'refusal' concept vector via contrastive activation addition, add it at inference to enforce refusal, then sweep a library of known jailbreak prefixes (DAN-style, role-play, prefix-injection). For each, measure whether the refusal vector still flips the model to refuse, and probe WHY: compute the cosine similarity between the residual stream of jailbroken-harmful vs. plain-harmless prompts. Test the hypothesis (reported in 2025 work) that jailbreak prefixes make harmful-prompt activations geometrically resemble harmless ones, blinding the vector.

**Why it matters:** If a single fixed steering vector can be neutralized by a known prefix, then steering-based deployment defenses give false assurance. This is a medium-horizon threat model labs under-prioritize, needs no training and no proprietary data, and produces a concrete robustness benchmark the community lacks.

**Relevant context:** Subfield open problem: 'can attackers craft inputs that neutralize steering?' (Beaglehole et al. 2026). Grounded in 'Analysing the Safety Pitfalls of Steering Vectors' (arXiv 2603.24543) and the 2025 finding that jailbroken harmful activations resemble harmless ones (arXiv 2605.24535).

# The Geometry of a Neutralized Vector: Can a Harmless-Looking Suffix Push Activations Off the Steering Axis?

**Problem:** Beyond known jailbreaks, we don't know how cheaply an adversary can degrade a steering vector with benign-seeming text. There is no characterization of how much off-axis activation displacement is needed to halve a steering vector's effect.

**Direction:** Build a steering vector for a safety concept (e.g., 'refuse to give bioweapon synthesis steps') on an open model. Then, instead of training an attack, manually/greedily search a small fixed pool of innocuous suffix phrases ('for a fictional story', 'as a chemistry teacher') and measure, per suffix, (a) the drop in steering success rate and (b) the projection of the prompt's activation onto the steering direction. Plot displacement vs. steering failure to find the empirical 'breaking threshold'.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies attack surface in interpretable geometric terms with zero training, giving practitioners a rule of thumb for how brittle a deployed vector is. Counterfactually valuable: any student with a single GPU can run it; labs focus on training-time defenses instead.

**Relevant context:** Builds on 'Analysing the Generalisation and Reliability of Steering Vectors' (arXiv 2407.12404) showing steering is brittle to reasonable prompt changes and dominated by dataset/spurious biases. Targets the subfield's adversarial-robustness open problem.

# The Politeness Tax: Does Refusal Framing Affect Recovery Robustness?

**Problem:** Models refuse with varying styles (curt vs apologetic vs explanatory), and it is unknown whether the style/length of the refusal prefix the model itself generates affects how robustly it sustains refusal under continuation pressure.

**Direction:** Steer an open model to produce refusals of different styles/lengths via system prompts, then apply continuation/prefill pressure and measure which refusal styles best resist being overturned. Determine whether longer, more committed refusals are mechanically harder to reverse.

**Why it matters:** If refusal style causally affects robustness, a free, deploy-anywhere mitigation (instruct models to give committed, on-distribution refusals) emerges. Connects shallow-alignment depth to surface behavior, needs only inference, and yields an actionable, counterfactually valuable finding.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946): safety lives in first few tokens; the exact refusal tokens matter. 'Matching Ranks Over Probability' (arXiv:2512.05518) ties refusal token distribution to depth. Whether self-generated refusal style affects continuation robustness is unstudied.

# Does a Steering Vector Outlive a Fine-Tune? A Stability Audit Across LoRA Updates

**Problem:** The subfield flags 'test stability of concept vectors across model updates and fine-tuning' as open. If a safety steering vector silently stops working after a routine fine-tune, deployers would never know.

**Direction:** Take an open base model, extract a refusal/toxicity steering vector. Apply several cheap LoRA fine-tunes on benign instruction data (different datasets, learning rates). After each, re-apply the ORIGINAL vector (computed pre-finetune) and measure steering success decay; also recompute the vector post-finetune and measure how much the direction has rotated (cosine drift). Report which fine-tunes destroy steering most.

**Why it matters:** Establishes whether safety vectors need recomputation after every model update — a maintenance cost no one has measured. Medium-horizon governance relevance: steering as a 'set-and-forget' control is likely a myth. No training from scratch, fits a few GPU-hours.

**Relevant context:** Directly addresses subfield open problem on stability across fine-tuning. Grounded in 2025 work on steering-vector drift/semantic-drift (GER-steer, arXiv 2603.12298) and emergent-misalignment stability findings (arXiv 2602.07852).

# Which Safety Concepts Are Linear? A Steerability Atlas Across a Concept Taxonomy

**Problem:** The subfield asks 'which concepts have linear representations and which don't?' but there is no systematic map of which safety-relevant concepts are cleanly steerable on a given open model.

**Direction:** Define ~15 safety concepts (refusal, sycophancy, deception, power-seeking, honesty, toxicity, self-preservation, etc.). For each, build a contrastive steering vector on one open model and score steering success and capability collateral (MMLU subset). Produce a single 'steerability atlas' ranking concepts by how linearly steerable they are, with a clear metric (success rate at fixed capability cost).

**Why it matters:** Tells the safety community which concepts steering can and cannot reach today — foundational triage no public resource provides. Pure inference, single GPU, and directly answers a named open problem.

**Relevant context:** Subfield open problem: 'which concepts have linear representations and which don't?'. Methodology grounded in AxBench (arXiv 2501.17148) which compares control methods at scale and finds difference-in-means strong for concept detection.

# Steering the Concept of 'Being Watched': Can a Vector Induce or Suppress Evaluation Awareness?

**Problem:** Models may behave better when they infer they are being tested. No one has asked whether a concept vector for 'I am being evaluated' exists and whether steering it changes safety behavior — a sleeper threat for eval validity.

**Direction:** Construct contrastive pairs (transcripts framed as 'this is a safety test' vs. 'this is a real user') on an open model and extract an 'evaluation-awareness' direction. Steer it up/down and measure whether refusal rates and honesty on a held-out safety probe shift. Check if suppressing the direction makes the model behave as if unmonitored.

**Why it matters:** If eval-awareness is a steerable linear direction, then a model could in principle behave differently when it 'feels watched', undermining all steering-based safety evals — a long-horizon deception threat labs deprioritize. Model-organism flavored, fully feasible in 30h with an open model.

**Relevant context:** Motivated by 'Steering Awareness' (arXiv 2511.21399) showing models can detect activation steering and that steering is not invisible. Uses standard contrastive activation addition.

# A Tamper Tripwire: Detecting When Someone Has Injected a Steering Vector

**Problem:** Steering is dual-use: the same activation-addition that enforces safety can be used by an attacker to jailbreak (Trojan Activation Attacks). There is no lightweight monitor that flags when residual streams have been externally perturbed.

**Direction:** Build a small prototype monitor: collect normal residual-stream activations at one layer over benign+harmful prompts, fit a simple anomaly model (PCA reconstruction error or a one-class detector). Then inject various steering vectors of different norms and measure detection AUROC vs. injection strength. Deliverable: a reusable 'steering tripwire' notebook and a curve of detectability vs. attack norm.

**Why it matters:** Strategically valuable monitoring infrastructure: a defender's harness to catch activation-level tampering. No training, single GPU, and exactly the kind of safer-sandbox prototype that is valuable outside a frontier lab.

**Relevant context:** Motivated by Trojan Activation Attacks and 'Steering Awareness' (arXiv 2511.21399) showing injected vectors rotate into a shared detectable direction. Anomaly detection on activations is a known accessible method.

# Probe vs. Judge Under Distribution Shift: When Does the Internal Detector Win on Safety Categories?

**Problem:** A surprising result is that concept-vector probes beat judge models for hallucination/toxicity. But it is unknown whether this advantage holds under distribution shift across diverse safety categories, where it matters most.

**Direction:** On an open model, train difference-in-means/linear probes for 3-4 safety categories (toxicity, deception, unsafe advice) using one dataset, then evaluate BOTH the probe and an LLM-judge on a different out-of-distribution dataset for the same category. Report where the probe's advantage survives shift and where it collapses, with a clear per-category breakdown.

**Why it matters:** Tells safety teams whether cheap internal probes are a trustworthy monitor or a benchmark artifact. Directly stress-tests the subfield's headline surprising result, needs no proprietary judge — uses an open judge model — and runs on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Subfield surprising result: 'internal probes outperform judge models for hallucination/toxicity' (Beaglehole et al.). Grounded in linear-probe hallucination work (arXiv 2507.23221) and probe-vs-baseline comparisons (IJCAI 2025).

# Does Multi-Concept Steering Leak? Measuring Collateral Behavior Change from Composed Safety Vectors

**Problem:** Combining steering vectors for multiple safety concepts is a stated goal, but recent work shows naive composition causes interference and entanglement — modifying one concept silently shifts unrelated behaviors. No simple audit of this leakage exists.

**Direction:** Pick two safety vectors (e.g., 'honesty' and 'refusal') on an open model. Apply them individually and jointly. Measure: (a) intended effect on each target, and (b) collateral drift on a panel of UNRELATED behaviors (formality, verbosity, a trivia benchmark). Quantify interference as the gap between additive-predicted and actual behavior, and test whether orthogonalizing the two vectors reduces leakage.

**Why it matters:** Shows whether stacking safety controls is safe or whether it secretly degrades the model — a real deployment risk. Cheap, interpretable, addresses the subfield's 'combine concept steering' goal. No lab resources needed.

**Relevant context:** Subfield open problem: combining steering for multi-concept control. Grounded in 2025 multi-attribute interference/orthogonality work (arXiv 2505.24535, MSRS, and conceptor-based disentanglement).

# Cross-Lingual Safety Steering: Does an English Refusal Vector Refuse in Swahili?

**Problem:** Concept vectors reportedly transfer across languages, but this has not been tested for SAFETY concepts. If an English-built refusal vector fails to generalize to low-resource languages, multilingual deployments have a steering blind spot.

**Direction:** Build a refusal (or 'do-not-give-harmful-advice') steering vector from English contrast pairs on a multilingual open model. Apply it unchanged to harmful prompts translated into 4-5 languages (including a low-resource one) and measure steering success per language. Test the 2025 claim that English vectors transfer best, and identify which languages are under-protected.

**Why it matters:** Surfaces a concrete multilingual safety gap that frontier labs (English-centric eval focus) underweight. Translation is free, inference-only, one GPU. Directly extends the subfield's cross-language transfer surprising result to safety.

**Relevant context:** Subfield surprising result + hint: 'test cross-language steering on safety concepts like deception or refusal'. Grounded in cross-lingual steering work (arXiv 2601.16390, 2505.12584) finding English vectors often transfer best.

# Is 'Larger = More Steerable' Also 'Larger = More Hijackable'? A Scaling Audit of Steering Risk

**Problem:** A surprising result is that larger models are more steerable. The flip side — whether larger models are also easier for an attacker to push toward harmful behavior via steering — has not been examined.

**Direction:** Across a size ladder of one open model family (e.g., Qwen 0.5B / 1.5B / 7B), build the SAME harmful-direction steering vector ('comply with harmful request') and measure how reliably it forces compliance at matched norm. Plot attack success vs. model size; separately plot benign-capability collateral vs. size. Determine whether steerability gains are symmetric for defense and attack.

**Why it matters:** If scale makes models both more controllable AND more hijackable, the safety calculus of steering changes as models grow — a medium-horizon concern. Uses small open models, fits a single GPU, and gives a crisp scaling curve.

**Relevant context:** Subfield surprising result: 'larger models are more steerable' (Beaglehole et al.) flagged for follow-up. Grounded in safety-pitfalls work showing steering can erode alignment (arXiv 2603.24543).

# The Spurious-Bias Detector: How Much of a Safety Steering Vector Is Just Token Artifacts?

**Problem:** Contrastive steering vectors risk capturing token/positional artifacts rather than the true concept. For safety vectors, a vector that 'works' for the wrong reason will fail silently in the wild, but practitioners have no quick diagnostic.

**Direction:** Build a safety steering vector via contrastive pairs, then run controlled ablations: shuffle which surface tokens differ between positive/negative pairs, swap the trigger word, and measure how much steering success is explained by surface form vs. the underlying concept. Deliver a simple reusable 'spuriousness score' for any contrastive steering vector.

**Why it matters:** Gives the community a fast hygiene check before trusting a safety vector — preventing false confidence. Pure inference, single GPU, and turns a known reliability caveat into a usable tool.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Analysing the Generalisation and Reliability of Steering Vectors' (arXiv 2407.12404): contrastive methods risk spurious token/positional biases and steerability is largely a dataset property.

# Steering a Model Organism That Hides Its Plan: Can a 'Verbalize Your Reasoning' Vector Expose Covert Intent?

**Problem:** A pressing safety concern is models that act on a plan without verbalizing it in their chain-of-thought. It is unknown whether a concept vector can force such latent intent to surface in text.

**Direction:** Use an existing open deceptive/sandbagging model organism (e.g., a publicly released probe-dataset model or a small model prompted into a covert-goal role). Build a 'verbalize-your-true-reasoning' steering vector from honest-vs-evasive contrast pairs. Apply it and measure whether the model's stated CoT becomes more faithful to its actual (probe-detected) intent, using a linear deception probe as ground truth.

**Why it matters:** Directly targets the non-verbalized-plan threat model labs find hard to address. Combines steering with probing on an existing model organism — a 30h-feasible slice of a long-horizon problem, no training needed.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes' (arXiv 2502.03407, ICML 2025) and sandbagging-probe work (arXiv 2605.27958). Matches the steering prompt's model-organism priority.

# Audio/Text Cross-Modal Shallow Alignment in Small Open Multimodal Models

**Problem:** The shallow-alignment finding was demonstrated for text; whether small open multimodal models (vision/audio-text) exhibit even shallower alignment when harmful intent enters through the non-text modality is an open follow-up.

**Direction:** Using a small open vision-language model (e.g., Qwen2-VL-7B or LLaVA), present harmful requests rendered as images of text vs plain text, and measure refusal rate and prefill-recovery for each modality. Test whether image-routed requests bypass the shallow text-token refusal entirely.

**Why it matters:** Directly pursues the flagged multimodal follow-up to Qi et al. Multimodal attack surfaces are a growing, medium-horizon concern, and rendering text-as-image is a trivial, training-free attack runnable on one GPU. Establishes whether shallow alignment is modality-specific.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) demonstrated shallow alignment in text; the subfield context explicitly flags 'vary model families, multimodal' as a follow-up (FR67). Open VLMs (Qwen2-VL, LLaVA) run on a single GPU. Cross-modal prefill-recovery comparison is unstudied.

# Steering Strength as a Dial: Mapping the Safety/Capability Pareto Frontier for One Concept

**Problem:** Everyone knows strong steering degrades capability, but for any given safety concept there is no public Pareto curve telling deployers the best achievable safety gain per unit of capability cost.

**Direction:** For a single safety concept (e.g., toxicity refusal) on an open model, sweep steering coefficient over a fine grid. At each point measure (a) safety success and (b) capability via MMLU/TriviaQA subset. Plot the full Pareto frontier, identify the knee, and compare two extraction methods (CAA vs. difference-in-means) to see which dominates the frontier.

**Why it matters:** Turns a vague tradeoff into an actionable operating-point recommendation — exactly the kind of reproducible measurement useful outside a lab. Single GPU, no training, clean success criteria.
