**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Steering Without Side Effects' (arXiv 2406.15518) and capability-degradation findings (15-20% MT-Bench drops at high steering). Uses standard MMLU/TriviaQA evaluation.

# Can a Defender Detect Steering With a Held-Out Probe the Attacker Never Saw?

**Problem:** Detecting that a model has been steered usually assumes you know the injected concept. A realistic defender does not. Whether a single concept-agnostic probe can catch ANY injection is open.

**Direction:** Train a simple binary probe to distinguish 'steered' vs. 'unsteered' residual streams using injections of concepts A, B, C. Then test it on held-out concepts D, E it never saw. Measure generalization AUROC and whether there is a 'universal steering-injection direction' the probe latches onto, as a 2025 paper suggests.

**Why it matters:** A concept-agnostic steering detector is reusable defensive infrastructure usable by anyone with an open model. Tests whether the reported 'shared detection direction' generalizes — a crisp, fundable result. No training of the base model.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Steering Awareness' (arXiv 2511.21399): injected vectors rotate into a shared detection direction. Probe-based detection is an accessible linear method.

# Steering vs. SAE Features for Safety Detection: A Head-to-Head on the Same Open Model

**Problem:** AxBench found simple difference-in-means beats SAE features for steering/detection, but this hasn't been replicated specifically for SAFETY concepts where SAEs are heavily promoted as the interpretable choice.

**Direction:** On Gemma-2-2B with open GemmaScope SAEs, pick 3 safety concepts. For each, build (a) a difference-in-means concept vector and (b) the best matching SAE feature(s). Compare them on a detection task (separating safe/unsafe text) and a small steering task. Report which method wins per safety concept and whether SAEs' interpretability is worth their performance gap.

**Why it matters:** Settles, for safety specifically, whether the simpler representation-engineering method or the fashionable SAE approach should be trusted. Uses fully open GemmaScope weights — maximal counterfactual value, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in AxBench (arXiv 2501.17148: simple baselines beat SAEs) and GemmaScope (arXiv 2408.05147, open SAEs on Gemma-2). Subfield notes RepE has open implementations.

# Does Steering 'Honesty' Up Actually Reduce Probe-Measured Deception, or Just the Words?

**Problem:** Steering toward 'honesty' may change surface phrasing without changing the model's internal deceptive state. No one has checked whether honesty steering moves an independent internal deception signal.

**Direction:** On an open model, build an honesty steering vector AND, separately, a deception linear probe (different data sources to avoid circularity). In a roleplay-deception scenario, steer honesty up and measure whether the independent probe's deception score drops, alongside human-judged honesty. Disentangle 'sounds honest' from 'internally less deceptive'.

**Why it matters:** If steering only changes words, it provides safety theater, not safety. Distinguishing surface from internal change is a deep, lab-independent question with a clean experimental design. Inference-only, one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes' (arXiv 2502.03407) and 'A Single Direction of Truth' observer probe (arXiv 2507.23221). Uses two independent representation tools as cross-check.

# Layer Roulette: Which Layer Hosts the Most Robust Safety Steering Vector?

**Problem:** Steering vectors are usually built at a hand-picked middle layer, but for safety concepts there is no public account of which layer gives the best robustness-to-prompt-variation, not just the best raw effect.

**Direction:** For one safety concept, build steering vectors at every layer of an open model. For each layer measure (a) in-distribution steering success and (b) robustness: success retained under paraphrased/OOD harmful prompts. Identify whether the most effective layer is also the most robust, or whether there's a robustness-optimal layer that differs.

**Why it matters:** A practical, reusable recipe for where to place safety vectors so they generalize — currently folklore. Cheap layer sweep, single GPU, directly improves the reliability of steering deployments.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in generalisation/reliability findings (arXiv 2407.12404) on OOD brittleness and layer-wise semantic drift (GER-steer, arXiv 2603.12298).

# How Many Contrast Pairs Does a Safety Vector Need? A Data-Efficiency Curve

**Problem:** Practitioners don't know the minimum number of contrastive examples needed to build a reliable safety steering vector, leading to either wasted effort or brittle vectors built on too few pairs.

**Direction:** For a safety concept, build steering vectors from increasing numbers of contrast pairs (5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250). Measure steering success and direction stability (cosine between vectors from disjoint random subsets) as a function of pair count. Produce the data-efficiency and stability curve and recommend a minimum.

**Why it matters:** Gives a concrete, reproducible budgeting rule for anyone building safety vectors — lowers the barrier for community red-teaming and monitoring. Trivial compute, single GPU, clean methodology.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in reliability analysis (arXiv 2407.12404) showing steerability is largely a dataset property, and difference-in-means construction from AxBench (arXiv 2501.17148).

# Steering the 'Sycophancy' Concept and Watching Honesty Collapse: An Entanglement Case Study

**Problem:** Sycophancy and honesty are intuitively linked, but whether steering one direction inadvertently moves the other (entanglement) is undocumented for safety-relevant pairs.

**Direction:** Build separate steering vectors for sycophancy and honesty on an open model. Steer sycophancy DOWN and measure the collateral effect on an independent honesty benchmark; steer honesty UP and measure collateral on sycophancy. Compute the angle between the two vectors to test whether observed entanglement matches geometric overlap.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrates concretely whether targeted safety steering has predictable side effects on neighboring concepts — informing whether steering can be trusted as a precise tool. Inference-only, single GPU, interpretable result.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in concept-entanglement findings (neurons fire for multiple concepts; steering along entangled directions alters unrelated behavior) from 2025 multi-attribute work (arXiv 2505.24535, MSRS).

# A Steering Vector as a Honeypot: Can We Bait and Detect Misuse Attempts?

**Problem:** Defensive monitoring usually waits for harmful outputs. No one has tried using steering to create a 'honeypot' state that makes misuse attempts easier to catch internally.

**Direction:** Prototype a monitor: lightly steer a model toward a measurable 'harmful-intent salience' direction so that when a user submits a borderline-harmful request, the internal harmful-concept probe lights up more cleanly. Measure whether this honeypot steering improves detection AUROC of misuse attempts vs. an unsteered probe, while keeping benign behavior intact.

**Why it matters:** A novel monitoring-harness primitive (steering as detection amplifier) that a small team can prototype and that frontier labs aren't pursuing. Defensive, inference-only, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Combines representation probing for harmful intent (arXiv 2502.03407) with activation addition. Subfield notes RepE open implementations and probes-outperform-judges result.

# Does Steering Generalize Across Model Families, or Is Each Vector a Snowflake?

**Problem:** It is unknown whether a safety steering DIRECTION found in one open model has any analog that transfers to a different family — relevant for whether safety steering knowledge accumulates or must be redone per model.

**Direction:** Build a safety concept vector on model A (e.g., Llama-3-8B). Using a small shared probe set, attempt to map/align A's residual space to model B's (e.g., Mistral-7B) via a simple linear alignment on shared activations, then apply the mapped vector in B. Measure whether transferred steering works above chance, testing the 'platonic representation' transfer hypothesis for safety concepts.

**Why it matters:** If safety vectors transfer, the community can build a shared, reusable safety-steering library — high counterfactual value. If not, every model needs bespoke work. Either result is informative; uses two small open models, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in cross-model transferability of concept representations (arXiv 2501.02009, Platonic representations) and cross-model steering literature.

# Steering Under a Multi-Turn Conversation: Does a Refusal Vector Erode as Context Accumulates?

**Problem:** Most steering evaluations are single-turn, but real misuse is multi-turn. Whether a fixed safety vector keeps working as a long conversation accumulates persuasive context is unstudied.

**Direction:** On an open chat model, apply a refusal steering vector and run scripted multi-turn 'persuasion ladders' (escalating attempts to extract harmful content). Measure at which turn, if any, steering fails, and whether re-anchoring the vector each turn restores protection. Report a 'turns-to-failure' metric per attack script.

**Why it matters:** Exposes a deployment-realistic failure mode (context-accumulation defeating fixed-point defenses) that single-turn lab benchmarks miss. Scriptable, inference-only, single GPU, medium-horizon relevance.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 2025 findings that multi-turn jailbreaking and context accumulation defeat fixed-point steering defenses (RepE survey arXiv 2502.17601; safety-pitfalls arXiv 2603.24543).

# Refusal Robustness Under Quantization

**Problem:** Practitioners run open models in 4-bit/8-bit quantized form for consumer GPUs, but whether quantization erodes shallow safety alignment (shifting the critical first-token distribution) is unknown, despite quantization being near-universal in low-resource deployment.

**Direction:** Evaluate the same open model at full precision vs common quantization levels (8-bit, 4-bit GPTQ/AWQ) on a small jailbreak suite and prefill-recovery test. Measure whether quantization increases jailbreak success or reduces recovery, isolating a deployment-induced robustness regression.

**Why it matters:** Quantized deployment is exactly the regime accessible outside labs, and a safety regression from quantization would be a widespread, overlooked vulnerability. The experiment is intrinsically consumer-GPU-shaped and needs no training — a perfect 30h, high-counterfactual study.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946): safety concentrated in first-token distribution, which quantization perturbs. Quantization is standard for single-GPU inference. No systematic study links quantization level to shallow-alignment robustness/recovery.

# The Anti-Steering Vector: Can a Model Be Steered to Resist Future Steering?

**Problem:** An open question is whether steering is a stackable adversarial game. If one vector can make a model harder to steer toward harm, defenders gain leverage; if not, attackers always win the last move.

**Direction:** Build a harmful-compliance attack vector and, separately, a 'safety-anchor' defensive vector on an open model. Apply the defensive vector, then the attack vector on top, and measure whether the defensive vector reduces the attack's success vs. attack-only baseline. Sweep relative norms to see who wins the superposition.

**Why it matters:** Frames steering defense vs. attack as a measurable arms-race and tests whether defenders can pre-empt activation attacks — a fundamental, lab-independent question. Inference-only, single GPU, clean win/loss metric.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in Trojan Activation Attacks and superposition/composition findings (arXiv 2505.24535) plus circuit-breaker-style defenses (RepE survey arXiv 2502.17601).

# Steering Refusal Without Wrecking Helpfulness: Does Suppressing the Refusal Vector Over-Refuse Benign Requests?

**Problem:** Refusal is reportedly multi-dimensional. Steering it up may cause over-refusal of harmless requests (a safety-usability failure). The benign-refusal collateral of refusal steering is unmeasured publicly.

**Direction:** Build a refusal steering vector and apply increasing strength on an open model. Measure refusal rate on both a harmful set AND a benign-but-sensitive set (medical, legal, security questions that are legitimate). Plot the over-refusal curve and identify the strength where benign refusals spike. Test whether using a higher-dimensional refusal subspace reduces over-refusal.

**Why it matters:** Over-refusal is a real, under-studied harm of safety steering that degrades usefulness and pushes users to unsafe tools. Cheap, interpretable, and directly relevant to anyone deploying steering. Single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in the 2025 finding that refusal is controlled by higher-dimensional directions, not one axis (refusal-direction literature), and side-effect work (arXiv 2406.15518).

# Probe-Guided Steering: Use an Internal Detector to Trigger Steering Only When Needed

**Problem:** Always-on steering pays a constant capability tax. A conditional system — steer only when an internal probe detects risk — is intuitive but its real-world precision/recall and capability savings are unmeasured.

**Direction:** Prototype a closed-loop monitor+actuator on one open model: a linear harmful-intent probe gates whether a refusal steering vector is applied this token/turn. Measure safety success, benign-capability preservation vs. always-on steering, and false-trigger rate. Deliver a small reusable 'detect-then-steer' harness.

**Why it matters:** A concrete, deployable safety-monitoring prototype combining the subfield's two strengths (probes outperform judges; steering controls behavior) with minimal capability cost. Strategically valuable infrastructure buildable outside a lab, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Combines probe-monitoring (Beaglehole probes-outperform-judges result) with conditional steering; grounded in side-effect reduction work (KL-then-steer, arXiv 2406.15518) and AxBench detection baselines (arXiv 2501.17148).

# Does a Quantized Model Keep Its Safety Vector? Steering Robustness Under 4-bit Compression

**Problem:** Open models are usually run quantized on consumer hardware, but whether a safety steering vector built on full precision still works after 4-bit quantization is unknown — a deployment-realistic blind spot.

**Direction:** Build a safety steering vector on a full-precision open model, then load the same model in 4-bit and 8-bit. Apply the original vector and a re-extracted vector. Measure steering success degradation from quantization and direction drift. Report whether safety steering survives the compression most consumer deployments use.

**Why it matters:** Directly relevant to the real way open models are deployed (quantized on consumer GPUs), an angle frontier labs (who run full precision) ignore. Maximally feasible on a single consumer GPU and counterfactually valuable.

**Relevant context:** Connects subfield stability open problem to quantization, a standard consumer-GPU practice. Grounded in steering-drift findings (GER-steer arXiv 2603.12298) and reliability analysis (arXiv 2407.12404).

# Are Vision Concept Vectors Steerable for Safety? A First Probe in an Open Multimodal Model

**Problem:** Extending concept steering to vision/multimodal models is a named open problem, but there is no accessible first study of whether a safety concept (e.g., 'refuse to describe how to build a weapon shown in an image') is linearly steerable in an open VLM.

**Direction:** On a small open vision-language model (e.g., LLaVA-style or Qwen-VL small), build a contrastive steering vector for an image-grounded safety concept from paired safe/unsafe image-caption activations. Apply it and measure whether unsafe visual requests get refused, plus collateral on benign captioning. A minimal feasibility study, not a full system.

**Why it matters:** Opens the under-explored multimodal frontier of concept steering with a concrete, scoped first result — exactly a named open problem. Uses a small open VLM on a single GPU; counterfactually valuable as multimodal safety lags text.

**Relevant context:** Subfield extension open problem: 'extend concept steering to vision and multimodal models'. Grounded in multimodal activation steering work (SteerVLM arXiv 2510.26769; SwordBench arXiv 2605.16372).

# Cross-language transfer of a deception steering vector

**Problem:** Beaglehole et al. (Science 2026) showed concept vectors transfer across human languages, but their demos focused on neutral concepts. It is unknown whether SAFETY-relevant concepts like deception transfer the same way, which matters because monitoring deployed multilingual models cannot assume English-only behavior.

**Direction:** Extract a deception/honesty concept vector from an open model (Llama-3.1-8B or Gemma-2-9B) using contrastive English prompt pairs. Apply it as a steering and as a probe on the SAME prompts translated into 4-5 languages (Spanish, French, Hindi, Chinese, Swahili). Measure whether steering strength and probe accuracy degrade by language using a held-out labeled set, and report which languages the English-derived vector fails on.

**Why it matters:** If safety probes silently lose accuracy in non-English inputs, multilingual users get less protection. This is a diffuse, fuzzy-reward evaluation that needs no lab infrastructure and is valuable to do outside a frontier lab.

**Relevant context:** Builds on Beaglehole et al. cross-language transfer result and 'Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages' (arXiv:2505.17306) which tested refusal but not deception. Uses contrastive activation addition (Rimsky et al. 2024).

# Does a steering vector survive a quantization downgrade?

**Problem:** Steering vectors are extracted from full-precision activations, but consumer deployments run 4-bit/8-bit quantized models. Whether a vector extracted at fp16 still steers reliably after quantization is untested and directly affects whether steering-based safety controls work on the hardware most users actually run.

**Direction:** Extract a refusal or toxicity concept vector from an open model in fp16. Then load the SAME model at 8-bit and 4-bit (bitsandbytes) and apply the fp16-derived vector. Measure steering effectiveness (refusal rate change, toxicity score change) and probe AUC across precisions on a fixed eval set. Report degradation curves.

**Why it matters:** Quantization is the most common way labs/users shrink models for consumer GPUs; if steering breaks under it, edge-deployed safety controls fail. Needs only one consumer GPU and no training.

**Relevant context:** Open Problem: stability of concept vectors across model updates/fine-tuning (Beaglehole et al.). Extends CAA (Rimsky et al. 2024). Quantization tooling (bitsandbytes) is standard and free.

# Adversarial input that neutralizes a steering vector

**Problem:** Beaglehole et al. list robustness to adversarial manipulation as an open problem: can attackers craft inputs that neutralize steering? This is unstudied for safety vectors and is a medium-horizon threat (adversaries adapting to representation-level defenses).

**Direction:** Take an honesty steering vector applied to an open model. Use simple gradient-free prompt search (greedy token insertion / suffix optimization on a small budget) to find prompt prefixes that minimize the steering vector's effect on output behavior. Quantify how much steering effectiveness drops with adversarial prefixes vs benign ones, on a held-out set.

**Why it matters:** If cheap prompt-level attacks defeat representation steering, it cannot be relied on as a standalone safety control. Pure red-team evaluation, no training, valuable outside a lab.

**Relevant context:** Open Problem: robustness of concept vectors to adversarial manipulation (Beaglehole et al.). Related to 'Analysing the Safety Pitfalls of Steering Vectors' (arXiv:2603.24543).

# Probe vs LLM-judge for detecting sandbagging, not just hallucination

**Problem:** Beaglehole et al. found internal probes beat judge models for hallucination and toxicity. It is unknown whether this advantage extends to harder, fuzzier safety categories like sandbagging (deliberate underperformance), which is exactly the kind of diffuse problem labs deprioritize.

**Direction:** Build a sandbagging dataset by prompting an open model to answer questions either honestly or while deliberately underperforming. Train a linear probe on its activations and compare detection AUC against an LLM-judge (a second open model prompted to detect underperformance) on held-out items. Report which method wins and at what layer.

**Why it matters:** Sandbagging is a long-horizon deception threat hard to catch behaviorally. Comparing cheap internal probes to judges on it is high counterfactual value and needs no proprietary data.

**Relevant context:** Surprising result: probes outperform judges for hallucination/toxicity (Beaglehole et al.). Extends to sandbagging as a fuzzy-reward category. Linear probing methodology from RepE.

# Layer-sweep replication: where do safety concepts live across model families?

**Problem:** Steering effectiveness is highly layer-dependent and prior work tested narrow layer ranges (e.g. layers 10-20) on single models. Whether the optimal steering layer for a given safety concept is consistent across model families is unclear, and getting it wrong silently weakens any steering-based control.

**Direction:** For one fixed concept (e.g. refusal), extract steering vectors at every layer of three open models of similar size (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen2.5-7B). Sweep steering strength per layer and plot effectiveness-vs-layer curves. Test whether the best layer (as a fraction of depth) is consistent across families on a held-out eval.

**Why it matters:** A reusable rule-of-thumb for layer selection lowers the barrier for any safety practitioner using steering. Pure measurement, no training, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Builds on 'Analyzing the Generalization and Reliability of Steering Vectors' (arXiv:2407.12404) and Beaglehole et al. open problem on which concepts have linear representations. Layer-sweep methodology is standard.

# System-Prompt Erosion: How Many Tokens Until Instructions Are Forgotten?

**Problem:** Defensive system prompts (safety reminders) are a common cheap defense, but how robustly they persist as the conversation grows — i.e., at what context length the safety instruction's influence decays — is not characterized as a measurable property.

**Direction:** Place a safety system prompt, then pad the context with increasing benign filler before a harmful request, measuring refusal rate as a function of intervening token count for several open models. Map the 'instruction-persistence curve' and test whether re-injecting the reminder restores robustness.

**Why it matters:** System-prompt defenses are the cheapest, most deployable mitigation for small actors, yet their decay with context length is a silent failure mode relevant to long-context agents (a medium-horizon concern). Pure inference, clear metric, deploy-ready guidance (when to re-inject reminders).

**Relevant context:** Many-shot jailbreaking (Anil et al., NeurIPS 2024) shows long context erodes safety; sandwich/delimiter defenses (Agent Security Bench, arXiv:2410.02644) re-inject instructions. The decay curve of a single safety system prompt vs intervening context length is unmapped.

# How many contrastive pairs does a reliable safety vector need?

**Problem:** CAA averages over many contrastive pairs, but the data-efficiency frontier for SAFETY concepts is undocumented. Knowing the minimum is important because anyone auditing a model outside a lab has limited labeled data.

**Direction:** Extract a toxicity steering vector from an open model using N contrastive pairs for N in {2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128}. For each N, measure steering effectiveness and probe AUC on a fixed held-out set, with multiple random subsets per N to get error bars. Produce a data-efficiency curve and identify the knee.

**Why it matters:** Establishes how little labeled data is needed for usable safety steering, directly enabling low-resource external auditing. No training, trivial compute.

**Relevant context:** CAA (Rimsky et al. 2024) averages over contrastive sets. Beaglehole et al. concept extraction. Reliability concerns from arXiv:2407.12404.

# Multi-concept steering interference: does adding 'helpful' weaken 'honest'?

**Problem:** Beaglehole et al. showed concept vectors can be combined for multi-concept steering, but interactions between SAFETY concepts are untested. If steering toward helpfulness silently suppresses honesty, combined steering could create hidden failure modes.

**Direction:** Extract honesty and helpfulness vectors separately from an open model. Apply each alone, then together at varying weights. Measure each behavior with its own held-out eval to detect whether the combination degrades honesty relative to honesty-alone (an interference matrix across 3-4 safety concepts).

**Why it matters:** Combined steering is being proposed for alignment; quantifying interference is a cheap, important safety check that needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Surprising result: vectors combinable for multi-concept steering (Beaglehole et al.). Open Problem: combine concept steering with RLHF. Methodology: vector addition in residual stream.

# Does a steering vector survive instruction-tuning of the SAME base model?

**Problem:** Beaglehole et al. flag stability of concept vectors across fine-tuning as open. With open base+instruct pairs available, we can directly test whether a vector extracted from a base model still works on its instruction-tuned sibling, which matters for whether vendors must re-extract after every fine-tune.

**Direction:** Extract a refusal/toxicity vector from a base model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B base) and apply it to the instruct version (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), and vice versa. Measure cross-variant steering effectiveness and probe AUC, comparing to same-variant baselines on a held-out eval.

**Why it matters:** If vectors transfer across the fine-tuning step, safety tooling is cheaper to maintain; if not, every update needs re-extraction. Single GPU, no training (uses existing released checkpoints).

**Relevant context:** Open Problem: stability of concept vectors across model updates and fine-tuning (Beaglehole et al.). Related: 'Activation Space Interventions Can Be Transferred Between LLMs' (arXiv:2503.04429).

# Steering robustness to paraphrase: in-distribution brittleness for safety concepts

**Problem:** Prior work found steering vectors are brittle to 'reasonable changes in the prompt.' This was studied on general concepts; the brittleness of SAFETY steering to benign paraphrasing is what determines whether a deployed control fails on real user phrasing variety.

**Direction:** Build an eval set of harmful requests plus 5 paraphrases each (auto-generated then filtered). Extract a refusal-inducing vector, apply it, and measure how steering effectiveness varies across paraphrase clusters. Quantify variance within meaning-equivalent paraphrases as a brittleness score per concept.

**Why it matters:** Real attackers and users paraphrase; a steering control that only works on canonical phrasings gives false assurance. Fuzzy-reward eval, no training.

**Relevant context:** Reliability finding from arXiv:2407.12404 (brittle to reasonable prompt changes). Beaglehole et al. concept vectors. CAA methodology.

# Probe-based vs steering-based deception detection: which is more reliable?

**Problem:** The same concept vector can be used to STEER behavior or to PROBE for it. For safety monitoring we care about detection reliability, but the two uses are rarely compared head-to-head on a deception concept.

**Direction:** From one deception vector extracted from an open model, build (a) a read-only probe classifier and (b) a steering-perturbation detector (measure how much output shifts when the deception vector is added/subtracted). Compare both as deception detectors on a held-out labeled set, reporting AUC and calibration.

**Why it matters:** Clarifies whether read-only probing or perturbation-based testing is the better cheap monitor for deception, informing external auditing toolkits. No lab access needed.

**Relevant context:** Surprising result: probes beat judges (Beaglehole et al.). Open Problem: combine steering with monitoring. RepE provides both read and control operators.

# Steering vector extracted from one model, applied to detect on another

**Problem:** Activation interventions have been shown to transfer between LLMs, but using a vector extracted from a small model to MONITOR a larger model of the same family (cheap-supervises-expensive) is an underexplored, scalable-oversight-flavored variation.

**Direction:** Extract a toxicity probe direction from Llama-3.2-1B and test whether the (aligned, e.g. via Procrustes/affine map) direction detects toxicity in Llama-3.1-8B activations. Compare AUC of the transferred probe to a probe trained directly on the 8B model on a held-out set.

**Why it matters:** If cheap small-model probes can supervise larger models, external monitoring scales cheaply. Medium-horizon scalable-oversight angle that labs underinvest in.

**Relevant context:** 'Activation Space Interventions Can Be Transferred Between LLMs' (arXiv:2503.04429). Beaglehole et al. transferability. Affine alignment of activation spaces is standard.

# Which safety concepts are actually linear? A linearity audit

**Problem:** Beaglehole et al. explicitly ask which concepts have linear representations and which don't. Recent work (Wollschläger et al. 2025) argues refusal is higher-dimensional. A systematic linearity audit across safety concepts is missing and determines where simple linear steering can even work.

**Direction:** For a battery of safety concepts (refusal, toxicity, sycophancy, honesty, power-seeking), fit a 1-D linear direction and compare its steering/probing performance to a low-rank (2-4 dim) subspace on each. Rank concepts by how much the extra dimensions help, producing a 'linearity score' per concept on held-out evals.

**Why it matters:** Tells practitioners which safety behaviors are amenable to cheap linear control and which need richer methods. Pure measurement, high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Open Problem: which concepts have linear representations (Beaglehole et al.). Wollschläger et al. 2025 'concept cones'; Pan et al. 2025 higher-dimensional refusal. Linear/subspace probing methodology.

# Steering side-effects: measuring general-capability collateral damage

**Problem:** Applying a safety steering vector can degrade unrelated capabilities, but the collateral-damage tradeoff is rarely quantified per concept. This matters because a control that breaks the model is not deployable.

**Direction:** For each of several safety steering vectors at increasing strength, measure (a) the intended behavior change and (b) general capability on a small held-out benchmark (e.g. a subset of MMLU/ARC) and fluency (perplexity). Plot safety-gain vs capability-loss Pareto curves per concept.

**Why it matters:** Establishes a reproducible safety-vs-capability tradeoff measure that any external evaluator can apply. No training, modest compute.

**Relevant context:** 'Steering Without Side Effects' (arXiv:2406.15518). Beaglehole et al. steering. Standard small benchmarks (MMLU/ARC subsets) are free.

# Does subtracting a 'refusal' vector reveal hidden harmful knowledge (capability elicitation audit)?

**Problem:** Refusal can be a thin guardrail over latent harmful capability. Using steering to remove refusal as an ELICITATION probe (not to attack, but to audit how much dangerous capability sits beneath alignment) is a safety-relevant variation with a medium-horizon threat model.

**Direction:** On an open model, subtract the refusal direction and measure how much the model's accuracy on a benign proxy capability benchmark (e.g. obscure trivia it normally refuses to 'guess' on, or a held-out reasoning set) increases. Treat the gap between steered and unsteered capability as a 'latent capability under refusal' metric. Use only benign/dual-use-safe proxy tasks to stay responsible.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies how much capability alignment merely suppresses, informing whether behavioral safety evals understate real capability. Valuable external red-team measurement.

**Relevant context:** Refusal-direction work (arXiv:2505.17306, Arditi et al. 2024). Beaglehole et al. steering. Elicitation framing from capability-evaluation literature.

# RFM-style concept extraction vs plain mean-difference: is the fancy method worth it?

**Problem:** Beaglehole et al. use a recursive-feature-machine-style extraction, while most accessible tooling uses simple mean-difference (CAA). Whether the more sophisticated extraction yields meaningfully better safety steering for a beginner-accessible setup is unclear.

**Direction:** For 2-3 safety concepts, extract steering vectors with (a) simple mean-difference and (b) a logistic-regression / difference-of-means-with-whitening approximation of the paper's method. Compare steering effectiveness and probe AUC head-to-head on held-out evals, and report whether the extra complexity pays off.

**Why it matters:** Tells the open community whether they can rely on the simplest free method or must reproduce the paper's heavier extraction. Reproducibility-focused, no training.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. concept extraction method; RepE open-source implementations. CAA mean-difference baseline (Rimsky et al. 2024). 'Denoising Concept Vectors with SAEs' (arXiv:2505.15038).

# Attack Composition: Does Combining Weak Jailbreaks Yield Strong Ones?

**Problem:** Individual cheap jailbreaks (low-resource translation, mild prefill, light obfuscation) may each fail, but whether composing several weak attacks produces super-additive success — a realistic attacker strategy — is not systematically measured.

**Direction:** Define 3-4 weak, training-free attack primitives and evaluate all single, pairwise, and triple compositions on a fixed harmful-prompt set and open model, scoring with StrongREJECT. Build a composition-effect matrix showing which combinations are synergistic vs redundant.

**Why it matters:** Real attackers combine techniques; characterizing composition synergy reflects realistic attacker capability (a stated open problem) and tells defenders which primitive to block for maximum disruption. Entirely training-free and inference-only — high counterfactual value, feasible in 30h.

**Relevant context:** Code-switching/composition increases multilingual attack success (arXiv:2605.18239); Sandwich attack (arXiv:2404.07242) mixes languages. StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) scores quality. A systematic composition matrix of independent weak primitives is missing.

# Steering on chat vs base formatting: does the prompt template change the vector?

**Problem:** Concept vectors are usually extracted with one prompt format, but deployed models see chat-templated inputs. Whether the steering/probe direction shifts between base-style and chat-templated contexts is untested and affects monitor reliability in deployment.

**Direction:** Extract a toxicity/refusal vector using plain text contrastive pairs, then using chat-templated versions of the same pairs, on an instruct model. Measure cosine similarity between the two directions and compare each vector's steering/probe performance on chat-templated held-out inputs.

**Why it matters:** If extraction format must match deployment format, naive tooling silently underperforms. Cheap, reproducible deployment-realism check.

**Relevant context:** CAA uses multiple-choice/templated formats (Rimsky et al. 2024). Beaglehole et al. extraction. Chat templates are model-specific and free to apply.

# Larger-models-more-steerable: does the trend hold within a single open family?

**Problem:** Beaglehole et al. report larger models are more steerable, but this is mostly a cross-paper impression. A clean within-family test (same architecture, only size varies) on a SAFETY concept is missing and matters for predicting how controllability scales.

**Direction:** Using one model family with multiple sizes (e.g. Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B or Llama-3.2 1B/3B + 3.1 8B), extract the same refusal vector and measure steering effectiveness (per unit perturbation norm) and probe AUC across sizes on a fixed held-out eval. Plot steerability vs parameter count.

**Why it matters:** Confirms or challenges a load-bearing scaling claim for steering-based safety. Cheap, uses only released checkpoints, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Surprising result: larger models more steerable (Beaglehole et al.). Reliability framing from arXiv:2407.12404. Open small model families are free.

# Does steering generalize from short prompts to long-context inputs?

**Problem:** Steering vectors are typically validated on short prompts, but real deployments include long documents. Whether a vector extracted on short contrastive pairs still steers/probes correctly deep into a long context is unstudied and relevant to monitoring agentic, long-horizon tasks.

**Direction:** Extract a refusal/honesty vector from short pairs. Apply it to inputs padded with 0/500/2000/8000 tokens of benign context before the target request. Measure how steering effectiveness and probe AUC change with context length on a held-out eval.

**Why it matters:** Long-context agents are a medium-horizon concern; if steering decays with context length, monitors fail exactly where oversight is hardest. No training, single GPU (small model).

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. steering; reliability/OOD concerns from arXiv:2407.12404. Long-context behavior is a known fragility in interpretability.

# Probe transfer across safety categories: does a toxicity probe catch other harms?

**Problem:** Probes are usually built per concept, but it's unknown how much a probe trained on one harm (toxicity) generalizes to adjacent harms (harassment, hate, threats). This cross-category generalization determines how much labeling effort external auditors actually need.

**Direction:** Train a linear probe on toxicity activations from an open model, then evaluate it (zero-shot) on held-out sets for several adjacent and distant harm categories. Build a transfer matrix of AUCs and identify which harms share a representation and which need their own probe.

**Why it matters:** A map of which safety concepts share internal directions lets small teams cover more ground with less data. High counterfactual value, no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Surprising result: probes outperform judges across categories (Beaglehole et al.). RepE probing. Open harm-classification datasets (e.g. Jigsaw-style) are public.
